system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by post-surgical malabsorption and hypoglycemia requiring continuous gastrostomy tube feeds presented with recurrent sharp pain at the G-tube site after running out of oxycodone, without fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, or tube feed intolerance. Exam showed a clean, intact tube site without erythema or induration, and labs/urinalysis were unremarkable. She was admitted overnight to the bariatric surgery service for symptom control, maintained NPO by mouth with continuous tube feeds, monitored closely without evidence of infection or bleeding, and her pain was managed with oral oxycodone with brief IV hydromorphone for breakthrough before transitioning back to oral-only therapy. She remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable, ambulatory, tolerating her tube feeding regimen, and was discharged home with instructions to resume home continuous feeds (NutriHep 50 cc/hr), monitor blood sugars, continue home medications, use PRN pain medications safely, and follow up with her surgeon.

having bowel movements and passing gas and is drinking water

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

You were admitted to ___ with 
pain at your G-tube site. You were given Oxycodone with good 
effect. Please resume your home continuous tube feeds (NutriHep 
@ 45 cc/hour). Continue to monitor your blood sugars when you 
return home.

Please call your doctor or nurse practitioner or return to the 
Emergency Department for any of the following:

*You experience new chest pain, pressure, squeezing or 
tightness.

*New or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or wheeze.

*If you are vomiting and cannot keep down fluids or your 
medications.

*You are getting dehydrated due to continued vomiting, diarrhea, 
or other reasons. Signs of dehydration include dry mouth, rapid 
heartbeat, or feeling dizzy or faint when standing.

*You see blood or dark/black material when you vomit or have a 
bowel movement.

*You experience burning when you urinate, have blood in your 
urine, or experience a discharge.

*Your pain in not improving within ___ hours or is not gone 
within 24 hours. Call or return immediately if your pain is 
getting worse or changes location or moving to your chest or 
back.

*You have shaking chills, or fever greater than 101.5 degrees 
Fahrenheit or 38 degrees Celsius.

*Any change in your symptoms, or any new symptoms that concern 
you.

Please resume all regular home medications, unless specifically 
advised not to take a particular medication. Also, please take 
any new medications as prescribed.

Please get plenty of rest, continue to ambulate several times 
per day, and drink adequate amounts of fluids.

Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery while taking pain 
medications.

Please follow up with your surgeon Dr. ___ at the 
appointment listed below.

Best wishes,
Your ___ surgical team

___

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. ___ from the bariatric surgery team. I understand you’re here for severe pain around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same pain again, but worse. I ran out of my oxycodone at home and Tylenol isn’t touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with this again. Any fever or chills? Any redness, drainage, or swelling around the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. The site looks the same to me—no pus or anything. It just hurts so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea or vomiting? Are you able to keep down water? And are you still tolerating your tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting. I can drink water. The feeds go in, but they irritate the area and make it ache more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you passing gas and having bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m going to examine the tube site now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The site looks clean—no redness or induration—and your belly is soft. It’s tender right at the tube, like you said. Your vital signs look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt this bad if it looks normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the frustrating part—pain can be severe even without an obvious infection or abscess. In the past, your CT scans showed nonspecific inflammation around the tube but no collection, and the tube exchange didn’t fix it. Tonight we’ll focus on getting your pain controlled safely and watching closely for any signs of infection or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried Naproxen because it actually helped, but then I was told to stop. Is it really that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—because of your gastric bypass history and prior marginal ulcer, NSAIDs like naproxen and aspirin can greatly increase the risk of another ulcer and bleeding. I want you to avoid them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then what am I supposed to do when the oxycodone runs out? I can’t live like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. For tonight, we’ll restart oral oxycodone and, if needed, use a small amount of IV hydromorphone for breakthrough pain while you’re here. The goal is to get you comfortable and then transition back to oral-only before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are you going to do another CT scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, since you don’t have fever, vomiting, or a change in the appearance of the site, and your exam is reassuring, we may not need repeat imaging tonight. We’ll check labs and keep reassessing—if anything changes, we’ll escalate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I just don’t want anyone to think I’m making it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you’re in real pain. Our job is to treat it and also keep you safe—especially with your history of ulcers and the tube dependence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your initial labs are back and look reassuring—blood counts and chemistries are stable, and there’s nothing suggesting infection or pancreatitis. We’ll continue to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s no sign of infection right now—no fever, no redness, and your labs don’t show a concerning pattern. We’ll keep watching your temperature and the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I keep my tube feeds running? I’m scared my sugar will drop if I stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll continue your home continuous tube feeds and monitor your intake and output. And keep checking your blood sugars like you do at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The feeds make the area sting. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some irritation can happen, especially if the area is already inflamed or sensitive. Since the skin looks okay, we’ll focus on pain control and make sure the tube isn’t causing skin breakdown.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The oxycodone helped some, but it’s still breaking through.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We can give a dose of IV hydromorphone for breakthrough pain now, but we’ll keep it limited and work toward stopping IV meds by later today so you can go home safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to be stuck here, I just need it controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our plan—short stay for symptom control, then discharge once you’re stable on oral medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the rest of the night after the breakthrough dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I slept a little. The pain is still there, but it’s not as unbearable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Today we’ll continue oral oxycodone as needed and stop the IV hydromorphone so we can make sure the oral regimen is enough for you at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’ll spike again once the IV is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it spikes, tell us right away—we’ll reassess. But we want to avoid IV opioids unless absolutely necessary, because they make discharge harder and can cause side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can drink water like you’ve been doing. Your nutrition is primarily through the continuous tube feeds, and we’ll keep that running.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to review safety steps while you’re here: we’ll use the leg compression devices and give you heparin shots to prevent blood clots, and we’ll encourage you to walk in the hallway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heparin shots again? Do I really need them for just a short stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—any hospitalization increases clot risk, even short ones. The dose is preventive and we’ll also get you up walking as much as you can.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by post-surgical malabsorption and hypoglycemia requiring continuous gastrostomy tube feeds was admitted to the bariatric surgery service for recurrent severe pain at the G-tube site after running out of oxycodone at home and being unable to control symptoms with acetaminophen; she briefly used naproxen with relief but stopped due to high marginal-ulcer risk. Exam showed a clean G-tube site without erythema or induration and a soft, non-distended abdomen; labs were reassuring and she remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable without evidence of infection or bleeding. She continued her home continuous tube feeds with monitoring, received DVT prophylaxis, and her pain was managed with oral oxycodone with short-term IV hydromorphone for breakthrough, then transitioned to oral-only therapy prior to discharge. She was discharged home ambulatory and stable with instructions to resume NutriHep continuous feeds at 45 cc/hr, monitor blood sugars, avoid NSAIDs, continue home medications, use PRN oxycodone safely, and follow up with her surgeon and planned specialty evaluations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it spikes, tell us right away—we’ll reassess. But we want to avoid IV opioids unless absolutely necessary, because they make discharge harder and can cause side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I allowed to eat anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can drink water like you’ve been doing. Your nutrition is primarily through the continuous tube feeds, and we’ll keep that running.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want to review safety steps while you’re here: we’ll use the leg compression devices and give you heparin shots to prevent blood clots, and we’ll encourage you to walk in the hallway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Heparin shots again? Do I really need them for just a short stay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—any hospitalization increases clot risk, even short ones. The dose is preventive and we’ll also get you up walking as much as you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood pressure is always low. Is that a problem with the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching it. Your pressures have been in your usual range and you’re alert, breathing well, and not dizzy. We’ll keep monitoring, especially with opioids on board.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How is your pain this afternoon on oral medication only?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. Still sore at the tube, but I can tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any new symptoms—fever, nausea, vomiting, or change at the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No. It looks the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s the long-term plan? I keep ending up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already in the middle of a longer work-up to find a solution. You have upcoming appointments for a second opinion with a bariatric surgeon, follow-up with Dr. ___, and a visit at the Pancreas and Liver Institute to discuss options including pancreatectomy for the hypoglycemia issues. Our role this admission is symptom control and making sure nothing dangerous is developing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pancreatectomy sounds extreme. Is that really on the table?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a specialized discussion and not a decision made during this short admission. The institute visit is to review your case and talk through risks, benefits, and alternatives. For now, we’re keeping your tube feeds steady and your sugars monitored.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve been afebrile and stable overnight. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but controlled with the oxycodone. I’m nervous about going home and running out again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you with a prescription for oxycodone 10 mg to take every four hours as needed for pain, with no refills. We’ll also review how to take it safely and when to call us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No refills—so what if the pain comes back before my appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your pain isn’t improving, is getting worse, or changes in character or location, you should call your surgeon’s office or come back to the ED—especially if there are red flags like fever, vomiting, black stools, or blood. We also want to avoid you using NSAIDs because of ulcer risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can you remind me what to watch for with ulcers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—vomiting blood or dark material, black or tarry stools, worsening abdominal pain, dizziness or fainting, or feeling very weak. If any of those happen, come in right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about infection at the tube site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Look for new redness spreading around the tube, warmth, swelling, pus-like drainage, worsening tenderness, or fever over 101.5°F. If you notice those, call or come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For your feeds, resume your home continuous regimen—NutriHep at 45 cc per hour—and keep monitoring your blood sugars at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I can do that. Can I drive myself home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not if you’ve taken oxycodone today. Avoid driving or operating machinery while on it. Please arrange a ride.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also continue your usual medications—like lansoprazole and sucralfate for ulcer protection, and your other home meds. Any questions about your medication list?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—no naproxen, no aspirin, no NSAIDs at all, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct—avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless a doctor specifically tells you otherwise, because of your marginal ulcer risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, I want to make sure you’re walking okay, urinating normally, and tolerating your tube feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been up walking, I’m peeing fine, and the feeds are running.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll discharge you home today. You’ll follow up with Dr. ___ as scheduled. If anything changes—fever, vomiting, dehydration, bleeding, chest pain, or worsening pain—call or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m still scared this will keep happening, but I understand the plan and the warning signs.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass complicated by post-surgical malabsorption and hypoglycemia requiring continuous gastrostomy tube feeds was admitted to the bariatric surgery service for recurrent severe pain at the G-tube site after running out of oxycodone at home and being unable to control symptoms with acetaminophen; she briefly used naproxen with relief but stopped due to high marginal-ulcer risk. Exam showed a clean G-tube site without erythema or induration and a soft, non-distended abdomen; labs were reassuring and she remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable without evidence of infection or bleeding. She continued her home continuous tube feeds with monitoring, received DVT prophylaxis, and her pain was managed with oral oxycodone with short-term IV hydromorphone for breakthrough, then transitioned to oral-only therapy prior to discharge. She was discharged home ambulatory and stable with instructions to resume NutriHep continuous feeds at 45 cc/hr, monitor blood sugars, avoid NSAIDs, continue home medications, use PRN oxycodone safely, and follow up with her surgeon and planned specialty evaluations.
